claim: Three opioid receptor subtypes have been established: μ (MOR), δ (DOR) and κ (KOR).
source: Through pharmacological and cloning experiments, three opioid receptor subtypes: μ (MOR), δ (DOR) and κ (KOR) have been established (Kieffer and Evans, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kieffer and Evans, 2009.

claim: Opioid receptors are found throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems with unique distributions for each subtype.
source: These receptors are found throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems with unique distributions for each subtype.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about opioid receptor distribution.

claim: Fluorescent ligands based on opioid peptides and opiate alkaloids often have decreased affinity and selectivity due to the addition of a fluorescent molecule.
source: Unfortunately, the use of these small-molecule ligands is often limited by the decrease in affinity and selectivity that results from the addition of a fluorescent molecule that is equivalent to or larger in size than the opioid ligand (Archer et al., 1992; Gaudriault et al., 1997; Madsen et al., 2000; Arttamangkul et al., 2000; Lam et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: β-naltrexamine has high binding affinity for all opioid receptor subtypes.
source: β-naltrexamine was chosen as the guide molecule (pharmacophore of the binding site) because it (1) has high binding affinity for all opioid receptor subtypes
evidence: The claim is stated as a reason for choosing β-naltrexamine as the guide molecule.

claim: β-naltrexamine has been used for conjugation with fluorescent dyes with minimal reduction in affinity.
source: β-naltrexamine was chosen as the guide molecule (pharmacophore of the binding site) because it (1) has high binding affinity for all opioid receptor subtypes, (2) has been used for conjugation with fluorescent dyes with minimal reduction in affinity (Emmerson et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Emmerson et al., 1997.

claim: β-funaltrexamine (β-FNA) irreversibly binds to MOR.
source: β-naltrexamine was chosen as the guide molecule (pharmacophore of the binding site) because it (1) has high binding affinity for all opioid receptor subtypes, (2) has been used for conjugation with fluorescent dyes with minimal reduction in affinity (Emmerson et al., 1997) and (3) is the parent compound of β-funaltrexamine (β-FNA), an affinity-labeling analog that irreversibly binds to MOR (Portoghese et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Portoghese et al., 1980.

claim: NAI-A594 bound to MOR, DOR and KOR with Ki ≈ 50, 70 and 200 nM, respectively.
source: Competitive radioligand binding assays showed that NAI-A594 bound to MOR, DOR and KOR with Ki ≈ 50, 70 and 200 nM, respectively (n = 2 of triplicate samples, see Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from competitive radioligand binding assays presented in Table 1.

claim: The linker for NAI was designed to be longer than that for β-FNA.
source: The linker for NAI was designed to be longer than that for β-FNA and was predicted to chemically modify nucleophilic side chains of amino acids on the extracellular loops 2 and 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NAI-A594 labeling of FMOR-expressing cells was stable after washing with naloxone.
source: Confocal images revealed the fluorescence of A594 and M1-A488 along the plasma membrane even after washing with the high affinity antagonist, naloxone (Figure 2A–a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2A-a.

claim: The fluorescence of NTX-A594 on plasma membrane was almost completely lost after naloxone wash.
source: The fluorescence of A594 but not of M1-A488 on plasma membrane was almost completely lost after the naloxone-wash (Figure 2A–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2A-b.

claim: NAI-A594 labeling of FDOR expressing cells was comparable to FMOR expressing cells after washing with naloxone.
source: After washing with naloxone (1 µM) the fluorescence of NAI-A594 on FDOR expressing cells was comparable to that in FMOR expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Persistent labeling of FKOR with NAI-A594 was negligible after naloxone wash.
source: Persistent labeling of FKOR was negligible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average fluorescence intensity of cells labeled with NAI-A594 (100 nM, 1 hr at 37°C) was similar to antibody labeling using M1-A594.
source: The average fluorescence intensity of cells labeled with NAI-A594 (100 nM, 1 hr at 37°C) was similar to antibody labeling using M1-A594 despite the fact that antibodies had an average four dye molecules per protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data described in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Application of naloxone (10 µM) decreased the average fluorescence intensity of NAI-A594 labeled cells by 30%.
source: Application of naloxone (10 µM) decreased the average fluorescence intensity by 30%, suggesting that there was a reversible component of NAI-594 labeling (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When naloxone was co-incubated during the labeling of NAI-A594 (100 nM), the average fluorescence intensity was reduced to only 2% of the NAI-A594 treatment alone.
source: When naloxone was co-incubated during the labeling of NAI-A594 (100 nM), the average fluorescence intensity was reduced to only 2% of the NAI-A594 treatment alone, indicating that non-specific staining was negligible.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data described in the text.

claim: Immunoblotting with anti-A488 detected a ~ 75 kDa band of FMOR only in cells labeled with NAI-A488 in the absence of naloxone.
source: Immunoblotting with anti-A488 detected a ~ 75 kDa band of FMOR only in cells labeled with NAI-A488 in the absence of naloxone (Figure 2C, left gel, lane 4), indicating that A488 was irreversibly bound to FMOR.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The attachment of A488 to purified FMOR increased with time and reached maximal intensity after 48 hr.
source: Analysis of in-gel fluorescence showed that the attachment of A488 to receptors increased with time and reached maximal intensity after 48 hr (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FMORs labeled with NAI-A594 were found co-localized with M1-A488 in the cytoplasm after [Met5]enkephalin (ME) application.
source: FMORs labeled with NAI-A594 were found co-localized with M1-A488 in the cytoplasm after [Met5]enkephalin (ME) application, indicating that the A594 labeled receptors could bind agonist, internalize, and be visualized in the endosomes (Figure 2F,a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Macroscopic images showed fluorescent signals in the area of LC after incubation with NAI-A594.
source: Following incubation, macroscopic images showed fluorescent signals in the area of LC (Figure 3A–a).
evidence: The claim is supported by macroscopic imaging data shown in Figure 3A-a.

claim: Fluorescence remained on LC neurons after application of naloxone (10 µM, 10 min).
source: Fluorescence remained after application of naloxone (10 µM, 10 min) indicating that the labeling was stable (Figure 3B–a').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-a'.

claim: Quantification of cell-associated fluorescence revealed a 40% decrease in the intensity of labeling after application of naloxone.
source: Quantification of cell-associated fluorescence revealed a 40% decrease in the intensity of labeling after application of naloxone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Labeling with the reversible ligand, NTX-A594, was not efficient and the fluorescence along the plasma membrane was nearly abolished after washing with ACSF for 10 min.
source: In contrast, labeling with the reversible ligand, NTX-A594, was not efficient and the fluorescence along the plasma membrane was nearly abolished after washing with ACSF for 10 min (Figure 3B–b,b').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-b,b'.

claim: There was no staining of NAI-A594 in LC neurons from MOR knockout rats.
source: There was no staining of NAI-A594 in LC neurons from MOR knockout rats (Figure 3B–c,c').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-c,c'.

claim: The labeling of NAI-A594 in the GFP positive neurons was blocked when slices were co-incubated with CTAP (1 µM).
source: The labeling of NAI-A594 in the GFP positive neurons was blocked when slices were co-incubated with CTAP (1 µM), a MOR-selective antagonist (Figure 3B–d').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-d'.

claim: Strong fluorescent labeling with NAI-A594 was found in the lateral parabrachial nucleus (PB).
source: In the same horizontal slices that contained the LC neurons, strong fluorescent labeling with NAI-A594 was also found in the nearby lateral parabrachial nucleus (PB, Figure 3A–a).
evidence: The claim is supported by macroscopic imaging data shown in Figure 3A-a.

claim: Labeled neurons in hippocampal formation (HC) were clearly visualized.
source: Lateral to the pons, labeled neurons in hippocampal formation (HC) were also clearly visualized (Figure 3A–a).
evidence: The claim is supported by macroscopic imaging data shown in Figure 3A-a.

claim: The fluorescent pattern in the hippocampus was very similar to that observed using MOR-specific immunohistochemistry in fixed tissue.
source: The fluorescent pattern in the hippocampus was very similar to that observed using MOR-specific immunohistochemistry in fixed tissue (Arvidsson et al., 1995a).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior immunohistochemistry work cited as Arvidsson et al., 1995a.

claim: Labeling of endogenous MORs with NAI-A594 was both concentration- and time-dependent.
source: Labeling of endogenous MORs with NAI-A594 was both concentration- and time-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: After incubation for 1 hr, labeling was observed with NAI-A594 at concentrations as low as 10 nM.
source: After incubation for 1 hr, labeling was observed with NAI-A594 at concentrations as low as 10 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: LC neurons having FMORs labeled with NAI-A594 were observed deep (90 µm) in the slice at a depth where visualization of FMORs labeled with M1-A488 was not well-defined.
source: LC neurons having FMORs labeled with NAI-A594 were observed deep (90 µm) in the slice at a depth where visualization of FMORs labeled with M1-A488 was not well-defined (Figure 3D–a,b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,a for quantification, and Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NAI-A594 labeling revealed a distinct distribution of fluorescent patches in coronal slices of striatum from mice.
source: In coronal slices of striatum from mice, NAI-A594 labeling revealed a distinct distribution of fluorescent patches (Figure 4-a,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4-a,d.

claim: Labeling in striatum was blocked when slices were co-incubated with CTAP (1 µM) indicating that NAI-A594 primarily labeled MORs.
source: Labeling was blocked when slices were co-incubated with CTAP (1 µM, Figure 4-b) indicating that NAI-A594 primarily labeled MORs.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4-b.

claim: Strong fluorescence induced by NAI-A594 was found in the thalamus and habenula.
source: Strong fluorescence induced by NAI-A594 was found in the thalamus and habenula (Figure 5-a,d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5-a,d,e.

claim: All the labeling in thalamus and habenula was absent in brain slices from MOR knockout rats.
source: Consistent with the results from the striatum, all the labeling was absent in brain slices from MOR knockout rats (Figure 5-b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5-b.

claim: Only ~3% of THGFP positive cells in midbrain showed staining with NAI-A594.
source: When midbrain slices were incubated in NAI-A594, only ~3% of THGFP positive cells showed staining with NAI-A594 (Figure 6A–a,c,c'; 3 out of 90 cells, eight slices, three animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The labeling of processes in midbrain was blocked by naloxone (10 µM) and CTAP (1 µM).
source: The labeling of these processes was blocked by naloxone (10 µM) and CTAP (1 µM, Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Application of NAI-A594 (500 nM) by circulating for 5 min caused a decrease of ME-activated GIRK current.
source: Application of NAI-A594 (500 nM) by circulating for 5 min caused a decrease of ME-activated GIRK current. The reduction was reversible after washing out of NAI-A594.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was no difference in the amplitude of currents induced by ME between labeled neurons and untreated cells in wild type rats.
source: There was no difference in the amplitude of currents induced by ME between labeled neurons and untreated cells in wild type rats (Figure 7B–b; Osborne and Williams, 1995; Levitt and Williams, 2012; Arttamangkul et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7B-b and citations to prior work.

claim: Following ME application, the fluorescence of NAI-A594 labeled receptors decreased along the plasma membrane and there were no clear fluorescent puncta in the cytoplasm.
source: Following ME application, the fluorescence of NAI-A594 labeled receptors decreased along the plasma membrane and there were no clear fluorescent puncta in the cytoplasm (Figure 7C–a,a').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 7C-a,a'.

claim: After ME application, fluorescent puncta of M1-A488 were found in the cytoplasm and clearly observed in the dendrites.
source: After ME application, fluorescent puncta of M1-A488 were found in the cytoplasm and clearly observed in the dendrites (Figure 7C–c,c').
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 7C-c,c'.

claim: NAI-A594 labeling did not disrupt the internalization of FMORs labeled with M1-A488.
source: The results indicated that while A594-linked receptors were not observed in the endosomes of LC neurons, NAI-A594 labeling did not disrupt the internalization of FMORs labeled with M1-A488.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that M1-A488 labeled receptors internalized normally in the presence of NAI-A594 labeling.

claim: NAI-A594 can be used in low nanomolar concentrations to label endogenous MORs.
source: This study shows that NAI-A594 can be used in low nanomolar concentrations to label endogenous MORs, thus providing the advantage of negligible non-specific background fluorescence and the absence of residual antagonism of NAI-A594 and its product.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing labeling at low nanomolar concentrations.

claim: An application of NAI-A594 at a high concentration of 500 nM took only 5 min to stain MORs of LC and PB neurons in the brain slice.
source: It should be noted that an application of NAI-A594 at a high concentration of 500 nM took only 5 min to stain MORs of LC and PB neurons in the brain slice thus indicating that NAI-A594 can efficiently label endogenous MOR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: NAI-A594 primarily and covalently labels MOR on neurons in brain slices.
source: Here we demonstrate that NAI-A594 primarily and covalently labels MOR on neurons in brain slices.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MOR has 12 amino acids that are potentially capable of reacting with fluorescent NAI, while KOR has 8 and DOR only 3.
source: For example, MOR has 12 amino acids that are potentially capable of reacting with fluorescent NAI, while KOR has 8 and DOR only 3.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of amino acid sequences shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The paucity of available reactive amino acids in DOR may be one factor contributing to lack of A594 modification in brain slices.
source: The paucity of available reactive amino acids in DOR may be one factor contributing to lack of A594 modification in brain slices, despite similar affinities of NAI-A594 for MOR and DOR.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observed selectivity of NAI-A594 for MOR over DOR.

claim: The density of DOR on the plasma membrane in vivo is lower compared to MOR.
source: It is possible that the density of DOR on the plasma membrane in vivo is lower compared to MOR (Wang et al., 2008 and references therein).
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: The selectivity of NAI-A594 for MOR makes this reagent a valuable tool to study the functionality and circuitry of MORs in many brain areas.
source: The selectivity of NAI-A594 for the MOR makes this reagent a valuable tool to study the functionality and circuitry of MORs in many brain areas.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The advantage of ligand-guided labeling is the ability to detect endogenous receptors in living slices.
source: The advantage of this ligand-guided labeling is the ability to detect endogenous receptors in living slices.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The labeling process is very simple and can be done in any buffer, at room or physiological temperatures and over reasonable time course.
source: The labeling process is very simple and can be done in any buffer, at room or physiological temperatures and over reasonable time course.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental methods described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Traceless affinity labeling uses a high affinity ligand to direct probe binding and ensure the labeling occurs near the ligand binding site.
source: In practice, a high affinity ligand is used to direct probe binding and ensure the labeling occurs near the ligand binding site.
evidence: The claim describes the principle of traceless affinity labeling as applied in this study.

claim: The close proximity between the ligand binding pocket and the reactive sites effectively increases the concentration of the reactive groups, enabling a probe of mild reactivity to be used.
source: The close proximity between the ligand binding pocket and the reactive sites effectively increases the concentration of the reactive groups, enabling a probe of mild reactivity to be used.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of traceless affinity labeling.

claim: The reactive probe of electrophilic acylimidazole (AI) has been shown to label a number of membrane-bound proteins, including folate, AMPA and GABAA receptors in living cells.
source: Among them, the reactive probe of electrophilic acylimidazole (AI) has been shown to label a number of membrane-bound proteins, including folate, AMPA and GABAA receptors in living cells (Fujishima et al., 2012; Yamaura et al., 2016; Wakayama et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The key covalent attachment of β-FNA at K233 side-chain was purposely avoided in the design of NAI.
source: The key covalent attachment of β-FNA at K233 side-chain was purposely avoided.
evidence: The claim describes a design decision in the synthesis of NAI.

claim: The carbonyl of acylimidazole can react with a nucleophilic side-chain of an amino acid that is Lys, Ser, Tyr and Thr.
source: The carbonyl of acylimidazole can therefore react with a nucleophilic side-chain of an amino acid that is Lys, Ser, Tyr and Thr (Fujishima et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fujishima et al., 2012.

claim: Once the transfer reaction occurs the dye remains attached to the receptor while naltrexamine moiety is free to dissociate.
source: Once the transfer reaction occurs the dye remains attached to the receptor while naltrexamine moiety is free to dissociate.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of traceless affinity labeling.

claim: Naltrexamine has a Ki of 0.26 ± 0.02 nM for MOR, 117.06 ± 8.94 nM for DOR, and 5.15 ± 0.26 nM for KOR.
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive binding assay data presented in Table 1, with reference to Li et al. (2009).

claim: The fluorescence of A594 from the reversible ligand NTX-A594 labeling was weaker compared to NAI-A594.
source: Images in (b) show the fluorescence of A594 from the reversible ligand NTX-A594 labeling was weaker and abolished following treatment with naloxone (1 µM, 10 min, n = 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2A-b.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of cells labeled with NTX-A594 (100 nM) was only 40% of that with NAI-A594.
source: The fluorescence intensity was only 40% of that with NAI-A594 and was further reduced with the application of naloxone.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data described in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No significant fluorescence was found in preparations of purified FMOR co-incubated with naloxone.
source: No significant fluorescence was found in preparations co-incubated with naloxone, indicating that this labeling was specific to FMOR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Increasing the concentration of NAI-A594 to 100 nM resulted in a well-defined florescent signal along the plasma membrane.
source: Increasing the concentration to 100 nM resulted in a well-defined florescent signal along the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Brain slices that were left in the incubation vials longer than 2 hr did not result in additional increased fluorescence.
source: Brian slices that were left in the incubation vials longer than 2 hr did not result in additional increased fluorescence (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: All three opioid receptor subtypes are found within the striatum and nucleus accumbens.
source: All three opioid receptor subtypes are found within the striatum and nucleus accumbens (Arvidsson et al., 1995b; Miura et al., 2007; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MOR is present predominantly in the striosomes or patches of the striatum.
source: MOR is present predominantly in the striosomes or patches.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about MOR distribution in the striatum.

claim: DOR and KOR are diffusely distributed throughout the striatum.
source: In contrast, DOR and KOR are diffusely distributed throughout the region.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about DOR and KOR distribution in the striatum.

claim: NAI-A594 did not efficiently label endogenous DORs in brain slices of the cortex.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, NAI-A594 did not efficiently label endogenous DORs in brain slices of the cortex where it has been shown to have DOR immunoreactivity (Cahill et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to prior immunohistochemistry work cited as Cahill et al., 2001.

claim: Dopamine cells in substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area are known to express KOR.
source: Dopamine cells in these areas are known to express KOR (Arvidsson et al., 1995b; Ford et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is a small population of dopamine neurons that are sensitive to ME and thus likely express MOR.
source: There is also a small population of dopamine neurons that are sensitive to ME and thus likely express MOR (Ford et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ford et al., 2006.

claim: Pre-application of NAI-A594 (500 nM) decreased receptor activation by nearly half.
source: We confirmed that NAI-A594 was an antagonist at MOR. Pre-application of NAI-A594 (500 nM) decreased receptor activation by nearly half while there was less than 10% inhibition by NAI-A594 at lower concentrations (30–100 nM, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data described in the text.

claim: The weak antagonism of NAI-A594 is probably due to the bulkiness of Alexa594 moiety.
source: Like other fluorescent small-molecule ligands, the weak antagonism of NAI-A594 is probably due to the bulkiness of Alexa594 moiety because NAI-AK, the reactive probe without the dye could significantly block MOR activation when used at 300 nM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A quenching phenomenon of A594 in the acidic environment of endosomes can be ruled out because the fluorescence of A594 is pH insensitive.
source: A quenching phenomenon of A594 in the acidic environment of endosomes can be ruled out because the fluorescence of A594 is pH insensitive (Panchuk-Voloshina et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Panchuk-Voloshina et al., 1999.

claim: Similar decline in fluorescence intensities of 30–40% was observed when either ME, morphine or naloxone were applied onto the labeled LC neurons.
source: Surprisingly, similar decline in fluorescence intensities of 30–40% was observed when either ME, morphine or naloxone were applied onto the labeled LC neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Flow cytometry results showed that a portion of labeling was displaced by naloxone.
source: This portion of labeling is competitive as also shown in HEK293 cells. Flow cytometry results also showed that a portion of labeling was displaced by naloxone (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The labeling induced by NAI-A594 allowed visualization of opioid-sensitive neurons in rat and mouse brains without loss of function of the fluorescently labeled receptors.
source: The labeling induced by this reagent allowed visualization of opioid-sensitive neurons in rat and mouse brains without loss of function of the fluorescently labeled receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript showing both visualization and functional responses.

claim: The ability to locate endogenous receptors in living tissues will aid considerably in establishing the distribution and physiological role of opioid receptors in the CNS of wild type animals.
source: The ability to locate endogenous receptors in living tissues will aid considerably in establishing the distribution and physiological role of opioid receptors in the CNS of wild type animals.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion about the potential impact of the developed method.
